bib.title: Syntriever: How to Train Your Retriever with Synthetic Data from LLMs

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Syntriever: How to Train Your Retriever with Synthetic Data from LLMs" (arXiv 2502.03824v3, 14 Feb 2025). First author Minsang Kim (Korea University and SK Telecom); corresponding author Seungjun Baek. No venue is printed, so call it a preprint. The reference-list format suggests an ACL-style submission, but the text never says so.

COVERAGE: Extraction was clean, 60,077 chars. I read chars 0 to about 44,500 in full (body, tables, limitations). The reference list after that I did not read line by line. The PDF has 16 pages (the extraction reports no page numbers). Appendices B to D (derivation, prompts, hyperparameters) are unread: the body cites them, and they were not in the part I read, so they may sit after the references. Figure images were not inspected. So this is not a read of all 16 pages; it is the body plus limitations.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Syntriever (E5-base, about 125M) beats 8 baselines on in-domain supervised BEIR sets, most on MS MARCO.
  number: 50.3 vs E5 42.4 nDCG@10 on MS MARCO (reported as "18.6%", a relative gain); HotpotQA 70.2 vs 63.4
  setup: BEIR, each model fine-tuned on that dataset's training set. All models about 125M. Syntriever trains on synthetic data generated from the training set. The LLM is GPT-4o (named in Sec. 3.6). The base encoder is E5.
  quote: "Syntriever improves the retrieval performances by: 18.6% on MSMARCO, 5.9% on HotpotQA, 2.5% on FiQA, 1.8% on SciFact, 8.3% on NFCorpus, and 4% on NQ."
  where: Sec. 3.2, Table 1
- In zero-shot transfer the gain is uneven and loses on several sets.
  number: best on 8 of 15 datasets, second on 1
  setup: Trained on synthetic data from MS MARCO and NQ, then evaluated on 15 BEIR sets. MS MARCO and NQ are in-domain for Syntriever.
  quote: "Table 2 shows that Syntriever achieves the best performances on 8, and the second best on 1, out of 15 datasets."
  where: Sec. 3.2, Table 2
  Losses read from Table 2: Arguana 38.8 vs BGE-M3 61.5; Climate-Fever 13.1 vs Nomic 27.0; Fever 60.2 vs Contriever 75.8 and BM25 75.3; Touche 19.9 vs BM25 36.7; SciFact 64.2 vs Contriever 69.3. BM25 still beats it on Fever, Touche and Climate-Fever.
- Hallucinated synthetic positives, relabeled as hard negatives, help. Roughly 15% of HotpotQA synthetic positives were relabeled.
  number: HotpotQA 67.4 to 70.2 nDCG@10; FiQA 40.8 to 41.9; SciFact 79.7 to 80.5
  setup: Ablation of self-verification and relabeling, Table 5. Relabel rates are given only as "approximately 15%" for HotpotQA and "a few percent" elsewhere.
  quote: "approximately 15% of synthetic positive passages were relabeled as hallucinations in the case of HotpotQA, whereas the proportion was about a few percent in other datasets"
  where: Sec. 3.5, Table 5
- The LLM-preference alignment stage adds the most, especially at the top rank. Distillation alone gives an average gain over the base retriever of 8.2%.
  number: alignment up to 8.8% gain. MS MARCO goes 46.2 (CoT plus synthetic, no alignment) to 50.3 (full). nDCG@1 gains are 3.8 to 10.5 points across encoders.
  setup: Table 3 ablation on 5 datasets; Table 4 with ColBERT, SBERT and Contriever base encoders (HotpotQA, FiQA)
  quote: "the distillation stage achieves an average gain of 8.2% over the base retriever" and "the alignment component (c+ ≻ c−) in Table 3 is shown to achieve performance gains of up to 8.8%"
  where: Sec. 3.3 to 3.4, Tables 3 and 4
- The partial Plackett-Luce loss beats Bradley-Terry alignment on harder sets.
  number: FiQA 41.9 vs 35.7; NFCorpus 43.3 vs 36.1; SciFact 80.5 vs 79.8
  setup: Table 8, nDCG@10. The authors' explanation, that BT lets the retriever forget distillation, is a hypothesis, not tested.
  quote: "BT model shows poor performances on FiQA and NFCorpus" and "BT model may cause the retriever to forget the knowledge learned during the distillation stage"
  where: Sec. 3.7, Table 8
- A weaker, cheaper LLM is competitive for synthesis, and a stronger one helps more for alignment feedback.
  number: Table 6 distillation only, NFCorpus nDCG@10 42.6 (4o-mini) vs 41.4 (4o); SciFact 76.3 vs 78.9. Table 7: HotpotQA nDCG@10 68.6 vs 70.2.
  setup: GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o, Tables 6 and 7
  quote: "smaller models may be better at teaching than larger ones in certain domains"
  where: Sec. 3.6
- Alignment top-K is a cost trade-off.
  number: K=5, N=10 pairs by default. FiQA nDCG@10 is 37.9 without alignment, 41.7 at K=3, 41.9 at K=5 and 42.5 at K=10.
  setup: Tables 9 and 10
  quote: "increasing K seems to exhibit diminishing returns on the performance"
  where: Sec. 3.8
- The "ground truth" labels are noisy, and synthetic positives are judged slightly better by GPT-4o.
  number: 88% of synthetic positives vs 84% of ground-truth passages "can derive answer"
  setup: 1000 random samples per set, judged by GPT-4o. HotpotQA is the cited example. The judge is the same family as the generator.
  quote: "GPT-4o states that only 84% of the ground truth passages have direct clues to the true answer"
  where: Sec. 3.9, Table 11
- The stated method: Stage 1 uses a modified soft-nearest-neighbour loss over 4 items: the query, the labeled passage, a synthetic positive, and a chain-of-thought sub-query text. The synthetic hard negative only repels.
  number: none
  quote: "there is no attraction term for synthetic hard-negatives (p−i ) in Ldistill(qi), i.e., they are used only for repulsion from other samples."
  where: Sec. 2.2

LIMITS
- The authors concede only the cost of LLM calls for synthesis and feedback. They argue cheaper models are catching up and give no dollar or call counts.
- Only about 125M encoders were tested, and only English BEIR with nDCG@10 (K varied only in the ablations). There are no latency, recall or end-to-end RAG-quality results.
- Comparisons are partly uneven. Baselines are published checkpoints, while Syntriever was trained on each dataset's synthetic data. Table 1 baselines may not have been fine-tuned per dataset, but this is not stated. The "up to 18.6%" is relative and sits on MS MARCO, an in-domain set.
- Zero-shot wins are not uniform (see the loss list under the zero-shot claim). The authors do not discuss the Arguana and Climate-Fever losses.
- Contamination is not checked. GPT-4o may have seen the BEIR corpora, and no result is reported for that.
- Table 4 base encoders were tested on 2 datasets only. Ablations were run on 5 datasets with a single seed, and no variance is reported.
- Dated: it positions itself against RePlug, which needs LLM output probabilities. "Black-box LLMs without logits" is the framing.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- InfoNCE: Oord et al., 2018; Izacard et al., 2021 (Contriever).
- Soft Nearest-Neighbor loss: Frosst et al., 2019.
- Hard negatives: Robinson et al., 2021.
- Chain-of-thought: Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022.
- RePlug: Shi et al., 2024.
- DPR: Karpukhin et al., 2020.
- E5: Wang et al., 2022.
- Preference modeling: Bradley and Terry 1952; Plackett 1975; Luce 1959; Ouyang et al., 2022 and Rafailov et al., 2024 (alignment).
- Synthetic-data embeddings: Wang et al., 2023 (Mistral-7B with GPT-4 data).
- Teaching with weaker models: Bansal et al., 2024.
- Larger negatives help: He et al., 2020.
- Self-verification: Weng et al., 2023.

CODE: None in the paper. The repository is github.com/kmswin1/Syntriever. The loss in Eq. 7 is the load-bearing form, but it is garbled in the extraction, so I did not copy it.

FIGURES (not extracted, so I give only caption text from the body)
- Fig 1, "Overview of Syntriever": Stage 1 synthesizes sub-queries, positives and hard negatives with a self-verification relabel branch. Stage 2 has the LLM compare pairs from the top K and trains with partial Plackett-Luce. It explains the two-stage pipeline faster than prose.
- Fig 2, "Example of LLM synthesis": a worked example of synthetic passages, with the correct answer in red.

NOTE CHECK (/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/03-keyword-semantic-and-hybrid-search.md, section "How embedders are trained, and where cosine misleads", lines 332 to 346)
- Already covered: InfoNCE and in-batch negatives, hard negatives and their cost ("how many and how hard is a measured question"), DPR, Promptagator (LLM-generated queries with a round-trip filter), Contriever, GTR, ModernBERT, rogue dimensions, FollowIR. A grep for "syntriever" finds nothing in the note. A grep of `references.md` for "syntriever|kim" returned only two unrelated rows (Wei et al. Skill-RAG, Zhao et al. LongRAG), so there is no Syntriever row.
- Not covered, and Syntriever adds:
  1. Black-box LLM data at both ends. Promptagator generates queries; Syntriever generates positives, hard negatives and an LLM pairwise-preference training signal, with no logits.
  2. Using the LLM's hallucinated positives as hard negatives. This is the strongest point because it is measurable: Table 5 gives +2.8 on HotpotQA, where about 15% of positives were flagged.
  3. A multi-positive loss over several labels per query, and a second-stage ranking alignment. Alignment lifts nDCG@1 most. Bradley-Terry alignment forgets (FiQA 35.7 vs 41.9).
  4. Some "ground-truth" labels are not answer-bearing: 84% are by one GPT-4o judge.
- Not about cosine misleading. The paper uses plain cosine with temperature and says nothing against it. It fits the "training and losses" and "Labels from an LLM" bullets, not the cosine-failure ones.
- If used, state these caveats in the note: E5-base, 125M, GPT-4o, BEIR nDCG@10, in-domain MS MARCO and NQ, and losses to BM25 on Fever, Touche and Climate-Fever.
